meta.title: Who really said "A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: A stock Roosevelt attribution with nothing behind it: no lifetime source, and no appearance at all in the digitised American newspaper record.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Theodore Roosevelt everywhere, sourced nowhere — the earliest citation anyone offers is a 1941 devotional book.

answer.label: Not Theodore Roosevelt — an unsourced attribution
answer.authorDates: earliest citation offered: a 1941 devotional volume
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this under “Disputed” ↗ on its Roosevelt page and offers a single citation — Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives (1941), a devotional volume published 22 years after Roosevelt died. We could find no earlier printing: the sentence returns no hits at all ↗ in the Library of Congress newspaper archive, in any wording we tried, and it appears in none of Roosevelt’s own digitised books.

source.heading: Where the line actually surfaces

docMeta.dd: No appearance found, in any wording
Disputed — no source in Roosevelt’s lifetime

source.excerpt: A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under “Disputed” ↗ on its Theodore Roosevelt page, with a lone citation to Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives (1941) — 22 years after Roosevelt’s death on 6 January 1919. We were unable to locate that volume to check it ourselves.

A search of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America archive returns no matches whatsoever ↗ for the sentence, and none for the looser variants “Bible is worth more than a college” or “Bible is better than a college education”. For a line this widely repeated, that silence across the digitised American press is striking.

The wording appears in none of the seven Roosevelt books we searched on Project Gutenberg — his Autobiography ↗, The Strenuous Life ↗, State of the Union addresses ↗ and four others. The phrase “college education” does not occur in any of them.

The one sourced passage in which Wikiquote ↗ records Roosevelt invoking scripture is a very different thing — a public-morality address closing on Proverbs 14, “Righteousness exalteth a nation” — and it makes no comparison between the Bible and a college.
source.excerptNote: The sentence is printed here as it circulates, because we found no earlier or fuller printing to quote from. Unlike most lines on this site, there is no period source to show you — and that absence is the finding.
source.rightsNote: With no identified author and no located first publication, no copyright or public-domain status can honestly be asserted for this wording.

author.name: Theodore Roosevelt
author.heading: About the credited author
author.bio: Theodore Roosevelt was president from 1901 to 1909 and one of the most prolific writers ever to hold the office — histories, natural history, memoirs, and a torrent of speeches and letters. He wrote and spoke about religion and public morality often enough that a line like this sounds unremarkable coming from him, which is exactly the problem: plausibility is not provenance, and none of that verified output contains this sentence.

cite.sourceCitation: No source from Roosevelt’s lifetime is known. Earliest citation offered by Wikiquote: Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives (1941) — a volume we were unable to examine. No printing of the sentence was found in Chronicling America, Library of Congress.

misattribution.heading: Who it’s wrongly credited to
misattribution.intro: The line circulates widely in devotional and inspirational writing — the earliest citation anyone offers for it is itself a devotional volume — always over Roosevelt’s name, and never with a source anyone can follow.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ classes it as disputed, offering only a 1941 devotional volume — two decades after his death. Nothing in his own books contains it, and we found no printing of the sentence anywhere in the digitised American newspaper record ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Until someone produces a Roosevelt source, this should be quoted as unattributed. Wikiquote’s disputed listing ↗ is the honest citation, and it is thinner than the quotation’s popularity suggests.

context.heading: Why the confusion
lead: Roosevelt invoked scripture in his public addresses — Wikiquote’s sourced material has him closing one on Proverbs 14, “Righteousness exalteth a nation” — so a crisp line ranking the Bible above a college degree slots neatly into the picture most people carry of him. Sayings attach to the names they suit.

What makes this one unusual is how completely the record is empty. Most disputed quotes at least leave a trail of early printings to argue over; this one leaves none, and the earliest citation anyone offers is a devotional book from 1941.
detailsBody: A caveat worth stating plainly: the 1941 volume Wikiquote cites was not available to us, so we cannot say what it claims or whether it names a source of its own. It may well credit Roosevelt without one, which is the usual pattern — but we have not read it, and we are not going to assert what is in a book we could not open.
context.pull: Most disputed quotes leave a trail to argue over. This one leaves none.
